power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Objective: Published Sepsis-3 detection rates range from 3.4 % to 65.2 % in MIMIC-III and from 9.8 % to 47.9 % in eICU-CRD.
We tested whether data preprocessing decisions alone produce differences of this magnitude when data, cohort and sepsis definition are held fixed.

Using the MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD databases we developed and applied a configurable pipeline (medalabel) that stepwise maps the databases into the OMOP Common Data Model, standardizes and cleans the data, and preprocesses them to compute Sepsis-3 labels.
Each setting of the preprocessing represents one decision of published Sepsis-3 implementations, and settings can be freely combined.

On fixed cohorts of first ICU stays (13,388 in MIMIC-III, 94,782 in eICU-CRD), we changed one setting of a reference configuration at a time (51 variants in five preprocessing domains) and compared detection rates and septic stays (Jaccard index) with the reference.
We approximately reconstructed six published pipelines and combined the settings with the largest effects in pairs to test whether their effects add up.
The time a value is measured can differ from the time it is documented and thus available for automated analysis.
Beyond the usual retrospective view based on measurement time, the pipeline optionally combines both time points to simulate a real-time system.
Results: The reference configuration labelled 31.5 % of ICU stays in MIMIC-III and 8.2 % in eICU-CRD as septic.
Changing a single setting resulted in sepsis detection rates of 15.3-58.6 % in MIMIC-III and 4.6-17.2 % in eICU-CRD.

The largest shifts from the reference, all in the same direction in both databases, came from the SOFA baseline, up to +27.1 percentage points (pp) in MIMIC-III and +9.0 pp in eICU-CRD, from disabling imputation (-16.3 and -2.5 pp), the temporal window (+12.6 and +5.3 pp) and aggregation (-10.1 and -0.8 pp); clinician-validated parameter sets had little effect (-4.8 and -1.1 pp).
Even variants that changed the rate by less than 2 pp labelled partly different patients, with Jaccard indices as low as 0.67 in MIMIC-III and 0.56 in eICU-CRD (1 = identical septic stays).
Reconstructions deviated from the published rates by 2-10 pp.
Two settings applied together deviated from the sum of their single effects by 0.9-11.8 pp in MIMIC-III and by up to 4.9 pp in eICU-CRD.
Simulating a real-time system lowered the MIMIC-III rate by 5.0 pp and delayed the label in 45 % of the stays that remained septic.
Discussion: With the infection criterion held fixed, preprocessing decisions alone can produce a considerable part of the variation between published sepsis detection rates.
Similar rates can stem from different patients, which makes studies and prediction models difficult to compare, and retrospective labels rely on values that a real-time system would not yet have.
Conclusion: Sepsis-3 labels from health records are only comparable if their data preprocessing is known.
Configurable pipelines allow quantifying the effect of these decisions, computing alternative labels on the same data and, in future, validating them against clinician-adjudicated cases.
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
Sepsis caused an estimated 11 million deaths in 2017, corresponding to 19 % of all deaths worldwide [1, 2], and it causes substantial in-hospital treatment costs [3].

text.text: Generally, sepsis-related research depends not only on correctly identifying sepsis cases but also on precise dates of sepsis onset.
The Sepsis-3 definition makes both possible, since the sepsis label and its onset can be computed directly from recorded clinical measurements.

In contrast, diagnosis codes are unreliable, as sepsis codes in US hospitals identified only 32.3 % of patients with severe sepsis or septic shock (as defined prior to Sepsis-3) confirmed by medical record review [13].

text.text: However, the Sepsis-3 definition leaves many implementation details open, such as which measurements to use, over which time windows to evaluate them and how to handle missing values.
Consequently, different implementations applied to the same data can yield substantially different sepsis labels.
This variability is illustrated by our recent review, which covered 64 Sepsis-3 implementations on MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD [14].

text.text: Sepsis detection rates ranged from 3.4 % to 65.2 % in MIMIC-III and from 9.8 % to 47.9 % in eICU-CRD, even among studies with identical cohort definitions.
Study characteristics such as the database, the unit of analysis and the infection detection method explained only about 9 % of this heterogeneity.

Based on the publications and the source code analysed in the review, we grouped data preprocessing and label computation methods into six domains: parameter selection for each SOFA component (D1), temporal windows (D2), aggregation (D3), handling of missing values (D4), SOFA calculation (D5) and identification of suspected infection (D6).
Most studies did not fully report how they implemented these six domains, and few published their source code.
As a result, neither the effect of individual decisions nor the reproducibility of published rates could be assessed [14].

text.text: Recent studies have also shown that varying components of the Sepsis-3 definition itself, such as the infection criterion or the timing of onset, changes both labels and prediction performance [15, 16].

text.text: In contrast, parameter selection, temporal windows and aggregation have not yet been varied on identical data.
To our knowledge, no study has compared single preprocessing decisions with a fixed reference, and no openly available pipeline exposes the decisions of domains D1-D5 as settings.
A further gap concerns time, because labels are computed retrospectively from the complete record, whereas a real-time system only sees values that have already been documented.
To address these gaps, we developed medalabel, a pipeline that maps ICU data to the OMOP Common Data Model [17] and exposes the preprocessing decisions of domains D1-D5 as configurable settings.

text.text: We hypothesized that single preprocessing decisions shift Sepsis-3 detection rates by an amount comparable to the variation between published studies, and that variants with similar rates label partly different patients.

In addition, we examined whether reconstructions of published pipelines reproduce their published rates, whether the effects of decisions from different domains add up and how much the labels rely on values that a real-time system would not yet have.

We developed medalabel (Figure 1), a configurable data processing pipeline based on the medallion architecture of data engineering, in which data pass through three layers of increasing quality called Bronze, Silver and Gold [18, 19].

text.text: It combines the preprocessing settings of published Sepsis-3 implementations in MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD in a single pipeline, so that each of them can be applied to either database.

The pipeline thus serves as a test bench for label computation, in which individual decisions can be varied while data, cohort and definition remain fixed and the labelling pipelines of published studies can be reconstructed.
Only the first layer is specific to a data source, and only the SOFA and label computation are specific to sepsis.
Each layer ends with an automated profiling step for quality control.
The technical specification is given in Supplement S1.
The Bronze layer maps the source data into the OMOP CDM v5.4 [17] without changing their content.

text.text: To simplify the following mapping to standard concepts, it fills the OMOP source_to_concept_map table with each source identifier, its name and, where the source data dictionary provides one, a standardized terminology code (LOINC, ICD-9, NDC).

Bronze profiling calculates statistics for each source parameter, such as the number of observations, value distributions and measurement frequency, and reports them separately for each recorded unit (e.g., FiO 2 in percent and as a fraction).
These statistics show clinical experts what a source parameter contains, even where its name is ambiguous or its unit is missing.
On this basis, the experts complete the mapping with standard OMOP concepts, unit rules, plausibility ranges and analytical tags, so that every standardization decision is clinically validated.
The Silver layer applies this annotated mapping through the assignment of standard concepts, normalization of units and removal of implausible values.
The Gold layer selects the cohort, stores it in the OMOP cohort tables and retrieves only the concepts tagged for the analysis, which determines the parameter selection (D1).

After normalizing vasopressor doses to body weight, deriving ventilation episodes and identifying suspected infection, the Gold layer applies four configurable stages, namely temporal aggregation by window size, step and per-parameter aggregation function (D2/D3), imputation of missing values (D4), SOFA subscore computation (D5) and Sepsis-3 label computation.

Imputation proceeds in three levels of increasing uncertainty: derivation from related parameters by established clinical relationships (e.g., total GCS from its components), estimation from earlier values of the same stay (e.g., forward filling) and, where no information exists, constant default values (e.g., normal values).
All settings are controlled through configuration files, so variants require no code changes.

On the technical side, the pipeline is started from a command line or scheduled with the workflow management software Apache Airflow, and it is packaged in Docker containers so that it runs unchanged on other systems.
To keep test cycles short, the pipeline was developed on the MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD demo datasets and then applied unchanged to the full databases.
More than 3,000 automated unit and integration tests (pytest test cases) check data integrity, transformation correctness and filter logic across all three layers.
In both databases, inclusion was restricted to adults (≥ 18 years) with an ICU stay of more than 24 h, and only the first ICU stay per patient was kept.

The effect of each variant was expressed as the signed difference between its detection rate and that of the reference in percentage points, and each domain was characterized by the difference between the highest and the lowest rate among its variants.

Two variants that do not correspond to a published method, the best-case aggregation (D3-S4) and the additional variant D2-S10, were reported but not counted in this difference (rationale in Supplement S2, Section S2.1).
Because all configurations run on the same fixed cohort, differences between them are exact and were compared without significance tests.
Because the cohorts are large, the sampling uncertainty of each rate is small (95 % Wilson confidence interval within ±0.9 pp of the rate), so confidence intervals are not shown for individual rates.
Shifts in SOFA total and subscores were summarized as mean differences from the reference (Supplement S2, Section S2.3).
Whether two configurations labelled the same stays was quantified with the Jaccard index, which is the number of stays labelled septic by both divided by the number labelled septic by at least one.
It is 1 when both label exactly the same stays and 0 when they share none, independent of whether the rates differ.
The index alone does not show whether a variant adds septic stays, removes them or exchanges them.
For every variant, Supplement S2 (Section S2.3) therefore also lists how many stays gained and how many lost the label compared with the reference.
Tier 3 interactions were computed as the observed effect of a combination minus the sum of the two single effects, in percentage points.
An interaction of 0 pp means that the effects simply add.
As an alternative, we compared the observed rate with the product of the relative changes of the two settings.

After applying the inclusion criteria, the reference cohorts comprised 13,388 ICU stays in MIMIC-III and 94,782 in eICU-CRD, with reference detection rates of 31.5 % and 8.2 %, respectively.
The catalogue of the 51 Tier 1 variants is provided in Supplement S2 (Section S2.1).
Before preprocessing, the Bronze layer held 21,813 source codes with about 365 million records in MIMIC-III, of which 349 codes were mapped to 39 OMOP concepts for the Sepsis-3 label.
In eICU-CRD, 255 of 14,276 codes with about 985 million records were mapped to 27 concepts.
Both databases recorded the same parameter under several names, codes and unit spellings.
In MIMIC-III, urine output had to be determined from 12 source codes named after the collection route (e.g., "Foley" and "Ileoconduit").
Mechanical ventilation was derived from 78 source codes.
In eICU-CRD, norepinephrine appeared under 19 names, some of which include the concentration, and a single platelet code carried 55 spellings of its unit.

Within an ICU stay, MIMIC-III recorded vital signs about hourly and laboratory values every 8 to 24 h on average, whereas eICU-CRD recorded SpO 2 about every 6 min and mean arterial pressure every 15 min, but laboratory values only every 15 to 37 h (Supplement S2, Section S2.2).
Detection rates varied widely across preprocessing configurations (Figure 2).

In these pairs, one setting dominated and the other lost much of its effect.

The 1 h blocks combined with mean aggregation (D2-S6 with D3-S2) labelled almost the same stays as the 1 h blocks alone (Jaccard 0.99), and the zero baseline combined with mean aggregation (D5-S15 with D3-S2) labelled almost the same stays as the zero baseline alone (Jaccard 0.94).
Conversely, the 1 h blocks, which raised the rate by 12.6 pp on their own, added less than 1 pp when no derivation or the zero baseline was applied as well (D2-S6 with D4-S2 and with D5-S15).
The stays they added were almost all labelled by the zero baseline already (92 % in MIMIC-III, 99 % in eICU-CRD), and without derivation only 8 % and 15 % of them remained septic.
A multiplicative model, in which the relative changes of the two settings are multiplied, did not fit better.
It came closer to the observed rate than the additive model in two of the six pairs in each database and deviated by up to 22.4 pp in MIMIC-III and 10.1 pp in eICU-CRD.

With data, cohort and Sepsis-3 definition held fixed, single preprocessing decisions shifted the detection rate from 31.5 % to between 15.3 % and 58.6 % in MIMIC-III and from 8.2 % to between 4.6 % and 17.2 % in eICU-CRD.

Variants with similar rates labelled partly different patients, reconstructions of published pipelines deviated from the published rates, the effects of two decisions rarely added up, and labels computed from measurement times relied on values that were documented only later.

A considerable part of the variation between published studies can therefore arise from the preprocessing decisions of domains D1-D5 alone, even with the infection criterion held fixed, which supports our first hypothesis.

Together with the reconstructions of published pipelines, which reached 25.9 % in eICU-CRD, our rates covered 70 % of the range published for MIMIC-III (3.4-65.2 %) and 42 % of that for eICU-CRD (9.8-47.9 %) [14].

text.text: These percentages compare only the lowest and the highest rate on each side.

In our analyses, these extremes come from single variants, in MIMIC-III from disabling imputation and from the zero baseline, and in eICU-CRD the highest rate comes from a reconstruction with its own cohort.
They should therefore not be read as the share of the published differences that preprocessing explains.
They show that preprocessing alone can move the rate across a similarly wide range.

The remaining range stems from studies that differ in what our design holds fixed, such as additional cohort filters, admissions instead of ICU stays as the unit of analysis, or an unreported infection definition [14], and from implementation details that our 51 variants do not cover.

text.text: In MIMIC-III, the baseline of the SOFA increase, the handling of missing values, the aggregation within a window, the window granularity, the restriction to the window around suspected infection and the exclusion of early-onset cases each shifted the rate by more than 10 pp, whereas the clinician-validated repository parameter sets mattered little (at most 4.8 pp).
In percentage points, eICU-CRD was less sensitive, but its reference rate is also lower.

Relative to the reference rate, the zero baseline and the 1 h windows had larger effects in eICU-CRD than in MIMIC-III (+110 % against +86 % and +65 % against +40 %), whereas disabling imputation and mean aggregation had smaller ones (-30 % against -52 % and -10 % against -32 %).
The direction of effects agreed between the databases whenever a variant mattered in both, but effect sizes did not transfer one-to-one.
Effects of decisions from different domains rarely combined additively.
When one setting dominated, such as the zero baseline or 1 h blocks, the other lost much of its effect.
This is partly inherent to the scale, because a stay can be labelled septic only once and two settings that act on the same stays cannot add their effects.
Effects of individual decisions therefore cannot simply be summed.
Our reconstructions approximate the published pipelines with the settings available in our pipeline.

Run on the same database version as the original studies, they yielded rates that deviated from the published ones by 2.2-9.5 pp in both directions, and these deviations cannot be attributed to a single cause.
Part of these deviations lies in the comparison itself.

Only one repository (Table 2, No. 1) reports both the number of septic cases and the cohort size, whereas for the other three the denominator had to be inferred from the size of the database [14], which tends to understate the rate when the published cohort was filtered further.

text.text: Yet even this repository, with both numbers reported, deviated by 5.7 pp.

The reconstructions also cover most, but not all, implementation decisions of the repositories (Supplement S2, Section S2.1), and published rates further depend on undocumented choices, software versions and extraction details that the code does not capture.
These results add a layer to known reproducibility problems.

Machine learning for health suffers from persistent reproducibility gaps [28, 29], and systematic reviews of sepsis prediction could not pool performance across studies because of varying sepsis definitions [30, 31].

text.text: In line with our second hypothesis, similar detection rates did not imply that the same patients were labelled.

Most variants relabelled only a small part of the stays, but some replaced about a fifth of the septic stays while leaving the rate almost unchanged, and the subscore analyses showed that variants act on specific organ systems.
Two studies with similar rates may therefore identify sepsis through different organ dysfunction patterns in partly different patients.
For prediction models, this may limit the comparability of reported performance and the transfer of published models to practice.
In observational and treatment-effect studies, the label decides which patients are analysed as septic, so estimates of incidence, outcome and treatment effect may inherit the same differences.
Every published label we examined, and our reference, also uses each value from its measurement time, as if it were available the instant it was recorded.
Counting values only once documented lowered the MIMIC-III rate by 5.0 pp.
About one in five septic stays of the reference lost the label, and in almost half of the remaining ones it was met later, so these labels depend on values that a real-time system would not yet have.
Because results from the laboratory table carry no documentation time, this is a lower bound.

text.text: Our results suggest that even a consensus definition does not yield consistent labels unless its operationalization is agreed and reported.
A common data model is necessary but not sufficient, because identical OMOP schemas can hold semantically different content [27] and identical data still yield different labels.

text.text: Mapping data into the model is itself demanding.
Even within one hospital, the same clinical concept was recorded under many source codes, and the 208 hospitals of eICU-CRD added local names, unit spellings and dosing conventions.
Such heterogeneity can be expected to grow with every additional site, and recording the mapping in a reviewable file, as in the Silver layer, makes this step transparent and reusable.

Labels would become comparable if studies reported at least the SOFA baseline, the handling of missing values, the aggregation rule, the window and observation period, the handling of early-onset cases, the information time and the parameter set of each SOFA component [14].

The reference requires a SOFA increase in addition to the diagnosis-based infection criterion, and in our reconstructions of the two eICU-CRD repositories this requirement lowered the rates by 2.5 and 4.0 pp.
The cohort differs as well, because the reference is restricted to first ICU stays of more than 24 h, and under the same requirement the cohorts of the two repositories yielded 16.8 % and 23.4 %.

text.text: Finally, our analyses show how much preprocessing changes the label, not which label is clinically correct, because neither database provides a clinical reference standard.
With data, cohort and infection criterion held fixed, the preprocessing decisions of domains D1-D5 changed how many and which patients were labelled septic by Sepsis-3 in two ICU databases.
The SOFA baseline had the largest effect in both databases, and the handling of missing values and the temporal window followed.
The effects of two decisions rarely added up, and in MIMIC-III retrospective labels relied on values that a real-time system would not yet have.
Sepsis-3 labels are therefore comparable only if their preprocessing is known.
We advocate routine sensitivity analyses of preprocessing and standardized reporting of the implementation decisions in domains D1-D6.
The configurable pipeline presented here makes these decisions explicit.
Which of the resulting labels is clinically correct remains to be tested against clinician-adjudicated cases.
